newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. to probe alleged cover-up in Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to probe alleged cover-up in Guatemala.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday decided to send a mission to Guatemala to probe accusations that the United Nations failed to investigate the killing of a guerrilla leader last year.

But U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said Annan considered such allegations "without foundation" and that Jean Arnault, the head of the U.N. operation in Guatemala, had himself requested "such an inquiry be conducted."

Eckhard said the fact-finding mission would be headed by Horacio Boneo, retired head of the U.N. election monitoring group, and would report directly to Annan. He said no date had been set but the visit would occur shortly.

"The secretary-general has been kept informed of press allegations against U.N. staff members in Guatemala in connection with the so-called Mincho case," Eckhard said. "We consider these press reports to be without foundation."
The accusations, which Arnault, a French diplomat, has denied, relate to the disappearance last October of guerrilla leader Juan Jose Cabrera Rodas, known as Commander Mincho.

Cabrera and a comrade, Augusto Rafael Baldizon, were involved in the kidnapping of an elderly woman that violated the terms of a truce and deeply embarrassed the Guatemala National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels.
The woman was released but the two guerrillas then disappeared. Baldizon later resurfaced, but in a rare show of unity both the government and the rebels denied for weeks that Cabrera even existed.

The United Nations Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala (MINUGUA) under Arnault concluded last week that elite army officials illegally captured and probably killed Cabrera during the final round of peace talks

Arnault helped broker an agreement ending the country's 36-year civil war that was signed on Dec. 29. International and local human rights groups have expressed concern that he or other U.N. officials knew of Cabrera's slaying but failed to investigate it because it might jeopardise the peace pact.

The rights groups as well as leaders of the former rebels also said they were dismayed that right-wing paramilitary groups, which were supposed to have been disbanded under the accords, were still operating, especially in rural areas.
Arnault told the New York Times on Friday that guerrilla leaders initially did tell him that one of their operatives in the kidnapping was missing.

When he then questioned government officials, he said, they appeared "absolutely convinced they did not have him." He said the allegations were part of a "stream of disinformation that has a lot to do with the perception of a dirty deal."
